"'''A Fifth of Beethoven'''" is a [[disco]] [[instrumental]] recorded by [[Walter Murphy]] and the Big Apple Band, adapted from the first movement of [[Ludwig van Beethoven]]'s [[Symphony No. 5 (Beethoven)|Symphony No. 5]]. The record was produced by [[production music]] and [[sound effect]]s recording producer [[Thomas J. Valentino]].<ref>{{cite news |title= Thomas J. Valentino Is Dead; Early Sound Effects Producer |date= August 6, 1986 |newspaper= [[The New York Times]] |access-date= April 23, 2010 |url= https://www.nytimes.com/1986/08/06/obituaries/thomas-j-valentino-is-dead-early-sound-effects-producer.html |archive-date= November 30, 2024 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20241130203430/https://www.nytimes.com/1986/08/06/obituaries/thomas-j-valentino-is-dead-early-sound-effects-producer.html |url-status= live }}</ref> The "Fifth" in the song's title is a [[pun]], referencing [[Fifth (unit)|a liquid measure]] approximately equal to one-fifth of a [[gallon]], a popular size for bottles containing [[liquor]], as well as Beethoven's Fifth Symphony from which the song was adapted.

Released as a single by [[Private Stock Records]] in 1976, the song debuted at number 80 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] chart and climbed to number 1 within 19 weeks, remaining there for one week. In 1977, it was licensed to [[RSO Records]] for inclusion on the best-selling ''[[Saturday Night Fever]]'' [[Saturday Night Fever (soundtrack)|soundtrack]]. The song is Murphy's only Top 40 hit.

"A Fifth of Beethoven" is a disco instrumental recorded by Walter Murphy and the Big Apple Band, adapted from the first movement of Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 5. The record was produced by production music and sound effects recording producer Thomas J. Valentino. The "Fifth" in the song's title is a pun, referencing a liquid measure approximately equal to one-fifth of a gallon, a popular size for bottles containing liquor, as well as Beethoven's Fifth Symphony from which the song was adapted.

Released as a single by Private Stock Records in 1976, the song debuted at number 80 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart and climbed to number 1 within 19 weeks, remaining there for one week. In 1977, it was licensed to RSO Records for inclusion on the best-selling Saturday Night Fever soundtrack. The song is Murphy's only Top 40 hit.

sections.heading: Background and recording
sections.wikitext:
In college, Murphy's interests included [[rock music]], particularly that which was adapted from [[classical music]], such as "[[Joy (Apollo 100 song)|Joy]]" (1971) by [[Apollo 100]] and "[[A Lover's Concerto]]" (1965) by [[The Toys]]. Later, in 1976, while writing a disco song for a commercial, a producer suggested the idea of "updating classical music", which "nobody [has] done lately".<ref>{{cite news|first= Mary |last= Campbell |title= Beethoven Arranger Having Ball |newspaper= [[The News and Courier]] |page= 48 |date= October 15, 1976}}</ref> He then recorded a demo tape of five songs—three were ordinary pop songs, while the fourth was a [[disco]] rendition of [[Beethoven]]'s [[Symphony No. 5 (Beethoven)|Fifth Symphony]] titled "A Fifth of Beethoven"<ref>{{cite news |first= Dave |last= Itzkoff |author-link= Dave Itzkoff |title= A Satirical Sit-Com's Memorable Music |newspaper= [[The New York Times]] |date= November 4, 2007 |access-date= December 6, 2016 |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/04/arts/television/04itzk.html |archive-date= May 15, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160515130052/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/04/arts/television/04itzk.html? |url-status= live }}</ref>—mailing it to various record labels in New York City.

The response was underwhelming, but "Fifth" caught the interest of [[Private Stock Records]] owner [[Larry Uttal]]. Murphy signed on to Private Stock and recorded the album ''A Fifth of Beethoven'', containing the title track and first single of the same name. The single was credited to "Walter Murphy & The Big Apple Band" upon encouragement from Private Stock, which believed it would be more successful if credited to a group rather than an individual. However, two days following the record's release, Private Stock discovered the existence of another Big Apple Band (which promptly changed its name to [[Chic (band)|Chic]]). The record was later re-released and credited to "The Walter Murphy Band", then simply to "Walter Murphy".<ref name="Superseventies">{{cite web |title= "A Fifth of Beethoven" by Walter Murphy |via= Superseventies |access-date= December 6, 2016 |url= http://www.superseventies.com/1976_7singles.html |archive-date= May 17, 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170517141850/http://www.superseventies.com/1976_7singles.html |url-status= live }}</ref>

The 1998 single "[[Enjoy Yourself (A+ song)|Enjoy Yourself]]" by [[A+ (rapper)|A+]] samples this song.

In college, Murphy's interests included rock music, particularly that which was adapted from classical music, such as "Joy" (1971) by Apollo 100 and "A Lover's Concerto" (1965) by The Toys. Later, in 1976, while writing a disco song for a commercial, a producer suggested the idea of "updating classical music", which "nobody [has] done lately". He then recorded a demo tape of five songs—three were ordinary pop songs, while the fourth was a disco rendition of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony titled "A Fifth of Beethoven"—mailing it to various record labels in New York City.

The response was underwhelming, but "Fifth" caught the interest of Private Stock Records owner Larry Uttal. Murphy signed on to Private Stock and recorded the album A Fifth of Beethoven, containing the title track and first single of the same name. The single was credited to "Walter Murphy & The Big Apple Band" upon encouragement from Private Stock, which believed it would be more successful if credited to a group rather than an individual. However, two days following the record's release, Private Stock discovered the existence of another Big Apple Band (which promptly changed its name to Chic). The record was later re-released and credited to "The Walter Murphy Band", then simply to "Walter Murphy".

The 1998 single "Enjoy Yourself" by A+ samples this song.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext: "A Fifth of Beethoven" started at number 80 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]; the single eventually reached number 1 within 19 weeks, where it stayed for one week. The single sold two million copies, while the album sold about 750,000 copies. The second single, a rendition of [[Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov]]'s "[[Flight of the Bumblebee]]", titled "Flight '76", reached number 44 on the Hot 100.<ref name="Superseventies"/>

sections.heading: In popular culture
sections.wikitext:
The music was used in a recruitment campaign by the [[Irish Defence Forces]] in the early 1980s.<ref>{{Cite news |last=O'Connell |first=Hugh |date=May 12, 2012 |title=Video: Why don't the Defence Forces make recruitment ads like this any more? |work=[[TheJournal.ie]] |url=https://www.thejournal.ie/video-why-dont-the-defence-forces-make-recruitment-ads-like-this-any-more-447560-May2012/ |access-date=February 23, 2023 |archive-date=February 24, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230224034901/https://www.thejournal.ie/video-why-dont-the-defence-forces-make-recruitment-ads-like-this-any-more-447560-May2012/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The song was used as the theme of the television miniseries ''[[Mrs. America (miniseries)|Mrs. America]]''.

The song was used in an episode of the second season of the TV series ''[[Pose (TV series)|Pose]]''.

An a cappella arrangement of ''A Fifth of Beethoven'' by [[Tobias Hug]] as recorded by [[The Swingles]], was used for the pilot episode of ''[[Glee (TV series)|Glee]]'', which was first aired on [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]] in May 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ingeniumacademy.com/tobias-hug |title=Tobias Hug |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=ingeniumacademy.com |access-date=September 8, 2024 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007091855/https://www.ingeniumacademy.com/tobias-hug |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.singers.com/performers/Tobias-Hug/ |title=Tobias Hug Biography |author=<!--Not stated--> |website=singers.com |access-date=September 8, 2024 |archive-date=August 14, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240814211020/https://www.singers.com/performers/Tobias-Hug/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The song was also used for a brief ''Saturday Night Fever'' parody that opened the 2006 ''[[Family Guy]]'' episode "[[Hell Comes to Quahog]]"; Murphy also composes the score for ''Family Guy''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://m.imdb.com/title/tt0828207/soundtrack/ |title=Hell Comes to Quahog – IMDB |access-date=February 5, 2025 |archive-date=April 17, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250417082320/https://m.imdb.com/title/tt0828207/soundtrack/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The instrumental was used during a montage in the series finale of ''[[Loki (TV series)|Loki]]'', "[[Glorious Purpose (Loki season 2)|Glorious Purpose]]".<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt18271352/soundtrack/ |title="Loki" Glorious Purpose (TV Episode 2023) – Soundtracks – IMDb |language=en-US |access-date=October 28, 2025 |via=www.imdb.com}}</ref>

The music was used in a recruitment campaign by the Irish Defence Forces in the early 1980s.

The song was used as the theme of the television miniseries Mrs. America.

The song was used in an episode of the second season of the TV series Pose.

An a cappella arrangement of A Fifth of Beethoven by Tobias Hug as recorded by The Swingles, was used for the pilot episode of Glee, which was first aired on Fox in May 2009.

The song was also used for a brief Saturday Night Fever parody that opened the 2006 Family Guy episode "Hell Comes to Quahog"; Murphy also composes the score for Family Guy.

The instrumental was used during a montage in the series finale of Loki, "Glorious Purpose".
